title: How did Gutenberg’s press spread books so fast?
hook: In fifty years, Europe went from hand-copied books to millions of printed ones.
summary: By printing from reusable metal type: from Mainz in the 1450s, presses spread across Europe and put millions of copies on the market by 1500.
cardText: Gutenberg combined reusable metal type, a sticky oil-based ink and a press, in Mainz in the mid-1400s. A page could be printed again and again, and by 1500 millions of copies were on sale.

cardBlocks.text: More and more readers wanted books, and many were still copied by hand. In Mainz, the craftsman Johannes Gutenberg brought three things together: metal letters that could be cast and reused, an oil-based ink thick enough to stick to metal, and a press probably adapted from those used for wine or oil. Once a page was set, it could be printed over and over.

His Bible, finished around 1455, proved the method worked. Then printing took off: by 1500 there were presses in some 60 German towns and at least 150 in Venice alone. One estimate puts about 20 million printed copies on the European market by the end of the century. In Brazil, the story only began in 1808.
Reusable metal type let printers make the same page many times; within fifty years, Europe’s presses had produced millions of copies.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Gutenberg was not the first to print with movable letters. In China, an artisan named Bi Sheng had invented movable type in the 11th century, and in 1377 Korea printed the Jikji, the oldest surviving book made with movable metal type. Gutenberg’s contribution was a whole system for Europe: type, ink and press working together.

Printing was expensive. Gutenberg borrowed large sums from a financier, Johann Fust, who later took him to court; in 1455 Gutenberg was ordered to repay the loans with interest. His Bible came out of that workshop in the mid-1450s, in more than 150 copies. About 40 survive, only some 20 of them complete.

Fifteenth-century presses produced roughly 27,000 to 30,000 editions. In the German lands, printed books overtook handwritten ones from 1469. With more readers came another change: more people needed spectacles.

In colonial Brazil, printing books was forbidden. Because of the Portuguese Crown’s obstacles, there was no official press until 1808, even though there had been several attempts to set up printing shops. When the royal family fled Napoleon, the first printing machines came with its fleet. On 13 May 1808, Prince Regent João created the Impressão Régia, the royal press, in Rio de Janeiro. On 10 September it began printing the Gazeta do Rio de Janeiro, the first newspaper printed in Brazil. Censorship of printers ended only in 1821.

claims.text: Johannes Gutenberg, a craftsman from Mainz, originated a method of printing from movable type.

claims.text: Gutenberg’s invention is thought to have combined a metal alloy for durable, reusable type, an oil-based ink thick enough to stick to metal, and a press probably adapted from wine, oil or paper presses.

support.excerpt: Elements of his invention are thought to have included a metal alloy that could melt readily and cool quickly to form durable reusable type, an oil-based ink that could be made sufficiently thick to adhere well to metal type and transfer well to vellum or paper, and a new press, likely adapted from those used in producing wine, oil, or paper, for applying firm even pressure to printing surfaces.

claims.text: Printed books appeared at a time when more and more readers wanted books, some of which were still copied by hand.

support.excerpt: Such works were completed at a time when books—some of which were still being hand-copied—were sought by an increasingly large number of readers.

claims.text: Gutenberg completed his Bible in Mainz in the mid-1450s, about 1455; more than 150 copies were printed.

support.excerpt: who completed it about 1455 working at Mainz, Germany.
In Mainz, Germany, in the mid-1450s, Johann Gutenberg and his partner Johann Fust published more than 150 large-format copies of the Bible in Latin.

The Anthology of Great Buddhist Priests’ Zen Teachings (1377), also known as Jikji, was printed in Korea 78 years before the Gutenberg Bible and is recognized as the world’s oldest extant movable metal type book.
